newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Congress and United Nations talk past each other.
newsitem.headline: Congress and United Nations talk past each other.

text.p: Minutes after U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan announced sweeping reforms for the United Nations bureaucracy on Wednesday, an influential U.S. senator said he was "underwhelmed" by the effort.

Annan, who became the U.N.'s top diplomat with U.S. backing six months ago because of his promises to institute reforms, presented a series of proposals to streamline the bureaucracy and urged governments to cut back programmes they were responsible for instituting.
Most nations and U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright complimented him on his proposals but reserved final judgment until they studied them in detail.

Sen. Rod Grams, Republican of Minnesota, said in a statement that Annan's reforms did not go far enough in cutting the entrenched bureaucracy at the United Nations and overcoming the vested interests of member states.

He said Annan did not "abolish a single programme," another reason Congress was linking paying of $819 million in U.S. arrears to specific conditions. The current U.S. debt to the United Nations is $1.6 billion.
But the U.S. Senate will only pay the $819 million if the United Nations meets a long list of conditions, some of which are bitterly opposed by the other 184 states.
Among the most controversial demand is reducing the U.S. share of the budget and crediting Washington with money it spent voluntarily to support peacekeeping missions.
"My assessment is that these unilateral demands do not impress, they do not intimidate, in fact they offend" the U.N. member nations, Annan said in answer to questions.
Other conditions say what the United Nations should be doing, which programmes or agencies should be abolished, and how many soldiers future peacekeeping missions should have.
Jeff Laurenti of the U.N. Association of the United States, a think-tank, believes Congress and the United Nations are "speaking two different languages, mutually incomprehensible."

He said "the anti-U.N. faction in Congress was not satisfied with anything other than a dramatic reduction of the U.N. role in the world, reducing it to functioning at the level of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, then asking why we need it at all."

New Zealand ambassador Michael Powles, speaking for Canada and Australia also, told the General Assembly that bold and innovative measures were needed or the United Nations would risk sliding into irrelevance.
But he said "we are not interested in mere cost cutting and we most emphatically disagree with suggestions which would leave the United Nations with a diminished role in the world."
